Recoil, shoulder and neck

Recoil is the backward push of the gun when it fires. You cannot avoid it, but recoil taken well should not hurt. Bruises on the shoulder, cheek or arm, or an aching neck after shooting, are a sign that something needs to change.

Coaches' experience

Felt recoil depends much less on strength than many beginners think. Many people give up after a first session because “it kicks so hard”. Often the cause is a gun that does not fit, cartridges that are too heavy or a poor mount, and all three can be changed.

Coaches' experience

A common cause is the mount. The stock should sit in the pocket of the shoulder, between the collarbone and the shoulder joint, and the cheek should rest firmly on the comb. Gun and body then move together, and the push spreads through the muscles instead of hitting one spot. If the stock sits on bone or on the arm, or there is a gap, recoil hits sharply.

Coaches' experience

Another cause is a gun that does not fit. A stock that is too long or too short makes you stretch the head and tense the neck. So does a comb that is too high or too low. A gun fit check with a coach or a gun fitter often helps quickly; see Gun fit basics. For juniors this matters even more: Equipment that fits a child.

Coaches' experience

Stance matters too. Keep the weight slightly on the front foot, lean a little forward and relax the shoulders. Leaning back lets the gun push you further. Hold the stock firmly in the shoulder, with no gap; see Stance: how to stand on the shooting stand.

Coaches' experience

Cartridges are another factor. In both disciplines FITASC rules allow at most 28 g of lead shot (up to 2% more is tolerated). In training many shooters use lighter loads, such as 24 g or 21 g, or low-recoil cartridges. For practice and for close to medium targets these are usually enough and far less tiring. On long targets a full load gives a denser pattern, the cloud of shot in the air, so more pellets reach the clay.

Coaches' experience

Recoil grows with the mass of the shot and its speed. Going from 28 g to 24 g at the same speed means about one seventh less shot, so the push is noticeably smaller.

Well researched

The weight of the gun matters as well. A heavier gun moves back more slowly, so the same cartridge feels softer.

Well researched

Many coaches add that a heavy gun also tires the arms sooner, so choosing the weight of a gun is a compromise.

Coaches' experience

A gas-operated semi-automatic uses part of the powder gas to reload, which spreads the push over a longer time. A recoil pad on the stock and a shoulder pad in the vest soften it further.

Coaches' experience

The neck suffers when you drop the head low or reach for the stock. Bring the stock up to the face and tilt the head only slightly. A light warm-up of neck and shoulders before shooting and between rounds may also reduce tension; see Warm-up and mobility.

Coaches' experience

Do not grit your teeth through pain. If your shoulder hurts, take a break or change to lighter cartridges. Pain can teach the body to jerk before the shot, a flinch, which is often harder to lose than a bruise. A coach can plan your training load so that shooting stays comfortable.

Coaches' experience

Safety: See a doctor or physiotherapist, rather than shooting through it, if pain lasts more than a few days. Do the same if you have numbness, tingling in the arm or severe neck pain.

Key points

  • Bruises and pain from recoil are a sign to change something, not “normal”.
  • Stock in the shoulder pocket, cheek firmly on the comb, weight slightly forward.
  • A gun that fits often reduces the pain quickly.
  • In training, lighter loads (24 g or 21 g) or low-recoil cartridges are usually enough.
  • Pain that lasts, numbness or tingling: see a doctor or physiotherapist.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. Where should the stock sit when you mount the gun?

    1. On the collarbone, close to the neck
    2. In the pocket of the shoulder
    3. On the upper arm, below the shoulder
    Answer

    In the pocket of the shoulder

    In the shoulder pocket the push goes into muscle rather than bone, and gun and body move together.

  2. What is the largest shot load that FITASC rules allow?

    1. 28 g
    2. 36 g
    3. 21 g
    Answer

    28 g

    Up to 28 g with a +2 % tolerance, in both disciplines; lighter loads are allowed.

    Chapter 7 · Cartridge rules

  3. Neck pain and arm numbness have lasted several days. What should you do?

    1. Shoot more to get used to it
    2. Use heavier cartridges
    3. See a doctor or physiotherapist
    Answer

    See a doctor or physiotherapist

    Persistent pain and numbness need to be checked by a specialist.

This is not medical advice.
